title: Singular & Plural Nouns
subtitle: The rules for making one into many — and a man who decided to become a knight.
objectives: Apply the y, f and o plural rules correctly
Recognise irregular plurals and nouns that do not change
Retell the opening of Don Quixote and explain what drives him

cards.title: Every game has an inventory
cards.text: One sword. Two swords. One knife. Two… knifes? No. English changes the rules on you, and there's a reason it does.

cards.title: Most nouns just take -s
cards.text: This is the rule that covers the vast majority of English nouns. Learn the exceptions and you've learned the whole topic.
points: **car → cars**, **helmet → helmets**, **bone → bones**
**No apostrophe. Ever.** Plurals never use one.
**car's** means something belongs to the car. Different job.

cards.title: Hissing sounds take -es
cards.text: If the word already ends in a hissing or buzzing sound, plain -s won't come out of your mouth. Say it aloud and you'll hear why.
points: **Ends in s, sh, ch, x or z** → add **-es**
**bus → buses**, **crash → crashes**, **punch → punches**
**box → boxes**, **buzz → buzzes**
**The test is your ear.** "Crashs" is unsayable.

question.explain: matches. It ends in -ch, so it takes -es. Try saying "matchs" — your mouth refuses.

cards.title: The y rule depends on what's before it
cards.text: Look at the letter immediately before the y. That single letter decides everything.
points: **Consonant + y** → drop the y, add **-ies**
**city → cities**, **story → stories**, **enemy → enemies**
**Vowel + y** → just add **-s**
**boy → boys**, **key → keys**, **day → days**

cards.title: Feed it a word and watch the rule fire
cards.text: Tap any word. The machine shows which rule caught it and why.

question.text: Which of these is spelled correctly?
question.explain: journeys. The letter before the y is **e**, a vowel — so it just takes -s. Only a consonant before the y triggers -ies.

cards.title: Some f words turn into v
cards.text: Words ending in -f or -fe often swap to -ves. Say them aloud and you'll hear the f soften.
points: **leaf → leaves**, **knife → knives**, **wolf → wolves**
**half → halves**, **life → lives**, **thief → thieves**
**But not always:** roof → roofs, chief → chiefs, belief → beliefs
**This one you memorise.** There's no trick.

cards.title: Words ending in o split two ways
cards.text: There's no rule you can reason out. Food words tend to take -es; music and shortened words take -s.
points: **-es:** potato → potatoes, tomato → tomatoes, hero → heroes
**-s:** photo → photos, piano → pianos, radio → radios
**Rough guide:** things you eat take -es.

question.explain: knives. The -fe becomes -ves. Same family as life → lives and wife → wives.

cards.title: The ones that ignore every rule
cards.text: These are older than the rules. English kept them because people used them too often to change.
points: **man → men**, **woman → women**, **child → children**
**foot → feet**, **tooth → teeth**, **mouse → mice**
**person → people**, **goose → geese**
**No pattern.** These are pure memory.

cards.title: Some never change at all
cards.text: One sheep, ten sheep. The word does the work and the number comes from context.
points: **sheep, deer, fish, aircraft, series, species**
**"Three fish"** is correct. So is "one fish".
**Watch the verb:** *the sheep **is** here* vs *the sheep **are** here*.

question.text: Put these plural rules in the order you'd check them for a new word.
items: Does it end in s, sh, ch, x or z?
Does it end in consonant + y?
question.explain: Check the odd ones first. Irregulars beat every rule, then the hissing sounds, then the y rule. Everything left over just takes -s.

terms.def: A word for a person, place, thing or idea.
One that follows a rule, like -s or -es.
One that ignores the rules, like child → children.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Grammar done. Part 2 is the story. It's about a man who read too many books and decided to become the main character. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Chapter 1: Getting Ready for Adventures
cards.text: A quiet gentleman in Spain owns a small farm, a skinny horse and a wall of books about knights. Then he makes a decision.

cards.title: He read himself out of reality
cards.text: Alonso Quixano read books about knights all day and most of the night. He sold farmland to buy more of them.
points: **He stopped sleeping** and stopped farming.
**He came to believe the books were history**, not stories.
**Then he decided** the world needed one more knight.

cards.title: This chapter is a character creation screen
cards.text: Every single thing he does in Chapter 1 is something you do before a playthrough starts.
points: **Picks a class:** knight-errant.
**Renames himself:** Don Quixote de la Mancha.
**Names his mount:** Rocinante.
**Chooses a lady to fight for:** Dulcinea del Toboso.

cards.title: The helmet he didn't test twice
cards.text: He built a helmet from pasteboard, tested it with his sword, and destroyed it in one blow. So he rebuilt it — and this time didn't test it.
points: **Rebuilt it with iron bars** inside.
**Then decided not to swing at it**, in case it broke again.
**He calls it perfect** and rides off wearing it.

question.text: Why doesn't Don Quixote test his second helmet?
options: He doesn't want to find out it's weak
He has run out of pasteboard
A knight told him not to
question.explain: He'd rather believe it works than know it doesn't. That choice tells you almost everything about him.

cards.title: Rocinante is a project car
cards.text: His horse is old, bony and slow. He spends four days deciding what to call it, and settles on Rocinante.
points: **He names it before he fixes it.** Sound familiar?
**The name has to sound grand.** That matters more to him than the horse.
**Then he spends eight more days** naming himself.

cards.title: Dulcinea doesn't know he exists
cards.text: A knight needs a lady to fight for. So he picks a farm girl from a nearby village, Aldonza Lorenzo, and gives her a nobler name.
points: **He renames her** Dulcinea del Toboso.
**They have never spoken.**
**He is not lying.** He genuinely sees her that way.

cards.title: This is how you start your own stories
cards.text: Your adventures always begin the same way: someone in a car, heading somewhere strange, about to meet something.
points: **Don Quixote does setup first.** Name, gear, mount, mission.
**Then he leaves.** The weird part starts after the setup, not before.
**Steal the structure.** It's four hundred years old and it still works.

cards.title: He isn't stupid. He's committed.
cards.text: Don Quixote isn't confused about what things look like. He decides what they mean, and then acts as if he's right.
points: **An inn becomes a castle.** A farm girl becomes a princess.
**He is the only one playing.** Everyone else sees an old man.
**Ask yourself all term:** is that madness, or is it courage?

question.text: Don Quixote gives new names to himself, his horse, and the woman he chooses.
question.explain: True. Alonso Quixano becomes Don Quixote, his horse becomes Rocinante, and Aldonza Lorenzo becomes Dulcinea. Naming is how he makes it real.

cards.text: Don Quixote was published in 1605 and is often called the first modern novel. The word quixotic — chasing something impossible because it's right — comes straight from him.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Default is -s.** Hissing sounds take **-es**.
**Consonant + y → -ies.** Vowel + y → just -s.
**Irregulars beat every rule:** child, foot, mouse, person.
**Don Quixote renames everything** — himself, his horse, his lady — to make the story real.

quiz.explain: boxes. It ends in -x, so it takes -es.
babies. The letter before the y is **b**, a consonant, so the y becomes -ies.
quiz.objective: Apply the y, f and o plural rules correctly

quiz.explain: monkeys. The letter before the y is **e**, a vowel — so it just takes -s.
quiz.objective: Apply the y, f and o plural rules correctly

quiz.explain: leaves. The -f becomes -ves, like wolf → wolves and half → halves.
quiz.objective: Apply the y, f and o plural rules correctly

quiz.text: Which of these is an IRREGULAR plural?
quiz.explain: teeth. The others all follow a rule. Tooth → teeth follows nothing — you just have to know it.
quiz.objective: Recognise irregular plurals and nouns that do not change

quiz.explain: False. Sheep doesn't change. One sheep, ten sheep — same word. So do deer, fish and aircraft.
quiz.objective: Recognise irregular plurals and nouns that do not change

quiz.explain: potatoes. Food words ending in -o usually take -es. Photos and pianos take just -s.
quiz.objective: Apply the y, f and o plural rules correctly

quiz.text: You use an apostrophe to make a noun plural, like **car's** for more than one car.
quiz.explain: False, and this is the most common mistake in English. Plurals never take an apostrophe. **car's** means something belongs to the car.

quiz.text: What was Don Quixote's real name before he renamed himself?
quiz.explain: Alonso Quixano, a quiet country gentleman. Rocinante is his horse and Aldonza Lorenzo is the woman he renames Dulcinea.
quiz.objective: Retell the opening of Don Quixote and explain what drives him

quiz.text: Why does Don Quixote decide to become a knight?
options: He read so many books about knights that he believed they were true
His family asked him to defend their land
quiz.explain: He read about knights day and night, and sold land to buy more books. Eventually he believed the stories were history.
quiz.objective: Retell the opening of Don Quixote and explain what drives him

quiz.text: What does Don Quixote name his horse?
quiz.explain: Rocinante. He spends four days choosing it, because the name has to sound worthy of a knight.
quiz.objective: Retell the opening of Don Quixote and explain what drives him

items: He reads books about knights until he believes them
He repairs old armour and makes a helmet
He chooses Dulcinea as his lady
quiz.explain: Books, then gear, then the horse, then the lady, then the road. He prepares his identity before he ever leaves the house.
quiz.objective: Retell the opening of Don Quixote and explain what drives him

teacher.summary: Week 1 English covers singular and plural noun forms plus Chapter 1 of Stories of Don Quixote Written Anew for Children by James Baldwin. The grammar half is ordered by which rule to check first, rather than as a flat list, so the learner has a procedure rather than seven things to remember. The literature half frames Chapter 1 as character creation, which is a genuine structural reading of the chapter and not only a hook.
discussion: Ask him to explain why 'monkeys' and 'babies' end differently. If he points at the letter before the y, he has the rule rather than the two examples.
Ask why Don Quixote doesn't test his second helmet. There is no wrong answer, and it is the question the whole novel is built on.
Ask whether Don Quixote is mad or brave. Keep the question open — it comes back every chapter this term.
Ask him to rename three ordinary things in the room the way Don Quixote would. It tests whether he understood that naming is how the character makes his world real.
teacher.extension: Have him write the opening of his own adventure using the same four moves: pick a name, pick a mount, pick something worth fighting for, and set off. Two hundred words. It rehearses Chapter 1's structure and it is the kind of writing he already does for fun.
misconceptions: 'Add an apostrophe to make a plural.' Never. Apostrophes mark possession or a missing letter, never number.
'All words ending in y take -ies.' Only after a consonant. Vowel + y takes a plain -s: boys, keys, journeys.
'All f words become -ves.' Many do, but roofs, chiefs and beliefs do not. These have to be learned individually.
'Don Quixote is simply stupid.' He is not confused about appearances — he decides what things mean and commits. That distinction is the point of the book.
